channel.title: B.I.A.S.
channel.description: Balanced Information, Actual Stories. Biased toward calm.

item.title: 'Squashed poo' a sign of water voles' success
item.description:
In a quiet corner of Surrey, conservationists are celebrating an unusual marker of success: squashed droppings along the muddy banks of the Hogsmill River. One year after releasing 42 water voles into this chalk stream, researchers have found compelling evidence that the population is not just surviving, but thriving. Urban rewilding officer Pia Trevelyan-Ashby spends her days searching for the telltale signs—Tic Tac-shaped droppings, burrows in the riverbank, and the peculiar phenomenon of "squashed poo," where water voles trample their own waste to mark territory using scent glands on their feet.
The return of water voles to the Hogsmill marks the end of a more than 20-year local extinction. These small rodents, immortalized as Ratty in The Wind in the Willows, have declined dramatically across the UK since the 1970s, with populations dropping by as much as 90 percent. The culprits include habitat destruction and predation by non-native mink, each of which can consume about one animal per day. The water vole reintroduction works alongside an intensive mink eradication program, creating conditions where the native species can reclaim their ecological niche. Camera traps and specially designed "latrine rafts" help researchers track the expanding population, which has now spread both upstream and downstream from the original release site.
This story offers a gentle reminder that conservation success often comes in unexpected forms. Water voles play a vital role in healthy river ecosystems, managing vegetation and serving as prey for larger species. Their presence signals improving river health and more naturalized habitats. Sometimes the most meaningful environmental victories are measured not in grand gestures, but in small, trampled droppings along a riverbank—quiet evidence that nature, given a chance, can find its way back.

item.title: 83-year-old VTuber posts wartime stories of Manchuria
item.description:
At 83, Kuniko Asai has found an unexpected medium for preserving history: she's a VTuber—a virtual YouTuber represented by an animated character—who shares wartime stories from Manchuria. Operating her channel "Manshu bachan" (Manchuria grandma) from Kanazawa, Japan, Asai appears as a bespectacled cat to recount experiences from World War II and the subsequent repatriation of Japanese people from northeastern China, where she was born.
Asai handles every aspect of video production herself, from research to filming, drawing on family stories and historical documents to explain the history of Manchuria and the lived experiences of those who returned to Japan. Her approach bridges a significant generational gap: as firsthand memories of the war era fade, she's translating them into a format designed for younger, digitally native audiences. The VTuber format, typically associated with entertainment and gaming content, becomes a vehicle for historical preservation.
What makes Asai's work quietly remarkable is the thoughtful collision of old and new it represents. She's taking some of the most painful chapters of twentieth-century history and presenting them through one of the internet's most contemporary storytelling forms. Her dedication—now three years into the project—speaks to a deep commitment to memory and education. In an age when historical events can feel distant or abstract, Asai's "Manchuria grandma" offers something personal and accessible, ensuring that stories of displacement, return, and survival don't disappear with the generation that lived them.

item.title: Research uncovers what determines flavour of Australian chocolate
item.description:
Australian researchers have uncovered a surprising twist in what makes chocolate taste the way it does: the location where cocoa beans are fermented matters even more than the cocoa plant variety itself. In trials conducted across three Far North Queensland sites—Mossman, Fishery Falls, and Mission Beach—scientists found that fermentation location could account for nearly half of a chocolate bar's final flavor profile, with each region producing distinctly different tastes.
The secret lies in the microorganisms naturally present in each environment. During fermentation, these tiny organisms produce metabolites that create flavor precursors, eventually transforming into notes ranging from fruity to chocolatey to buttery. Because Australian cocoa fermentation relies on naturally occurring microbes rather than controlled yeast strains, the local environment plays an outsized role. The Mossman beans developed fruity notes, Mission Beach cocoa emerged more traditionally chocolatey, and Fishery Falls fell somewhere between. University of Queensland food chemist Marlize Bekker explained that these environmental microorganisms and their metabolic processes are the key drivers behind the regional variation.
This discovery could reshape how Australian chocolate is marketed and enjoyed. Industry leaders envision a future where chocolate carries regional designations similar to wine appellations, allowing consumers to choose based on terroir-driven flavor profiles. For Australia's emerging premium cocoa industry, this research offers both scientific validation and commercial opportunity—a way to justify premium pricing while celebrating the distinct character that comes from a specific place and its invisible microbial residents. It's a quiet reminder that flavor is as much about location and process as it is about the raw ingredient itself.

item.title: Survivors Reunite with Pets After Earthquake in Colombia
item.description:
In the aftermath of a devastating 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck Colombia, killing 273 people and injuring more than 3,800, a quieter story of hope is unfolding amid the rubble. While rescue teams race against the critical 72-hour window to find survivors, a dedicated group of volunteers has taken on a different mission: reuniting displaced families with their beloved pets trapped in the wreckage.
Vickye Giraldo, a 56-year-old lawyer in Cali, experienced an "indescribable moment" when volunteers pulled her cat Polux from the ruins of her destroyed apartment building. She had four pets inside when the earthquake hit; one dog was rescued, another animal died, and one remains missing. The emotional reunion, captured as Giraldo kissed Polux's head with tears in her eyes, reflects the profound bond between people and their animal companions during crisis. Volunteer Nelson Vidales explained his motivation simply: "We know that pets are like children," adding that while many focus on human victims, animals also deserve representation and rescue efforts.
With more than 12,000 homes destroyed and thousands of families displaced, these animal rescues offer moments of joy within an immense tragedy. Another dog, visibly weakened, received immediate veterinary care after being pulled from debris to spontaneous applause. Andrea Paredes continues to hope her dog and cats, trapped in her bathroom when the earthquake struck, might still be found alive. These stories remind us that in disaster's wake, compassion extends in all directions—and that the smallest reunions can restore hope when everything else has been lost.

item.title: Big Bear Valley’s beloved bald eagle Jackie is dead
item.description:
Jackie, a fourteen-year-old bald eagle from California's Big Bear Valley, has died after three weeks of intensive veterinary care. Found grounded and fighting with juvenile eagles in mid-July, she arrived at the Ojai Raptor Center severely dehydrated and anemic. Despite treatment including a blood transfusion, she developed blood clots in her wing and kidney that led to her death in early August.
Jackie and her mate Shadow became global celebrities through a livestream camera perched 145 meters high in a Jeffrey pine, installed by Friends of Big Bear Valley. Since 2018, millions of viewers worldwide watched the pair mate, raise chicks, and weather storms in real time. A dedicated Facebook page with 1.3 million followers chronicled every milestone and heartbreak, while teachers across the country streamed the nest in classrooms, using Jackie's family as a living lesson in wildlife and resilience. Together, the eagles successfully raised seven chicks, with each year's offspring named by local third graders.
Jackie's influence extended beyond education and entertainment. Her popularity sparked a remarkable conservation effort: more than 25,000 donors contributed $10 million to purchase 63 acres of Jackie and Shadow's habitat that had been slated for luxury housing development. Her remains will go to the National Eagle Repository, where they'll be distributed to tribal members for ceremonial and educational purposes. This story matters because it shows how a single bird, made visible through technology, can forge genuine emotional connections across continents and inspire tangible conservation action—a quiet reminder that caring begins with seeing.

item.title: One of Australia's longest-serving editors dies aged 96
item.description:
Robin Letts, who died at 96, spent nearly eight decades with The Buloke Times in Donald, Victoria—a family newspaper founded by his ancestors in 1875. His commitment to the paper was remarkable: he began working there in 1947 at age 17, became editor in 1987 after his father's death, and continued working six days a week until a fall earlier this year finally curtailed his duties. Even then, he retained his title and remained dedicated to the publication until his passing.
Letts was more than an editor; he was a cornerstone of his community. Colleagues and readers remember him for writing with honesty and heart, eschewing sensationalism while covering every local group and story with care. His mentorship shaped generations of journalists, and his 2003 Medal of the Order of Australia recognized both his service to Donald and his commitment to community journalism. The Buloke Times, under the Letts family stewardship, became Australia's longest continuous family newspaper dynasty, surpassing even the Fairfax legacy before being sold in late 2023.
This story quietly honors a disappearing breed: the local editor who knows everyone in town, tells their stories with integrity, and remains at his post for a lifetime. In an era of consolidating media and shrinking local newsrooms, Letts's 79-year tenure stands as a testament to what community journalism can mean when rooted in genuine care and unwavering presence.

item.title: The Guardian view on solar eclipses: moments of wonder that bring us together | Editorial
item.description:
When a partial solar eclipse swept across Britain on Wednesday, crowds gathered to witness the familiar sun dim into an eerie twilight, temperatures drop, and the landscape take on an otherworldly cast. One observer in Cornwall captured the experience as "magical eeriness"—a blend of beauty and wrongness that won't recur in Britain for another 55 years. For those fortunate enough to stand in the path of totality across Greenland, Iceland, and Spain, the spectacle was even more profound: a black disc surrounded by a fiery corona against a purple sky, a sight Britain won't see again for 64 years.
Humanity's relationship with eclipses traces a fascinating arc from fear to understanding. Ancient civilizations saw celestial dragons or demons devouring the sun, while a Greek philosopher in 478 BC first proposed the correct explanation. That knowledge later became a tool of power, as when Columbus used his prediction of a lunar eclipse to coerce food from Indigenous Jamaicans. By the 19th century, Britain's imperial apparatus had transformed eclipse chasing into serious science, with expeditions discovering helium during an 1868 eclipse in India and, most famously, confirming Einstein's theory of relativity during the 1919 eclipse observed from West Africa and Brazil.
What makes this story quietly remarkable is its reminder of our shared humanity. In a fractured world, eclipses still draw us together in collective wonder, transcending national boundaries and individual concerns. The 1919 expedition's ironic outcome—British scientists elevating a German physicist to global fame just after a devastating war—shows that some phenomena belong not to any single nation, but to all of us. These moments of cosmic alignment offer both spectacle and perspective, inviting us to look up from our divisions and remember what we hold in common.

item.title: Land rights and mangroves entwine in a Brazilian quilombo’s resistance
item.description:
Along Brazil's Atlantic coast, where the São Francisco River flows into the sea, a collection of traditional Afro-Brazilian communities known as Brejão dos Negros is fighting for land rights that have eluded them for generations. Officially recognized as quilombos—settlements founded by formerly enslaved people and their descendants—in 2023, these communities still await the land titles they've been demanding for two decades. While the federal land reform agency has demarcated more than 8,000 hectares of their territory, residents have been authorized to use less than a tenth of it, leaving them vulnerable to encroachment and environmental degradation.
The story of Brejão dos Negros is one of layered injustice and resilience. The region, once called Refúgio dos Negros for its role as a sanctuary for escaped enslaved people, became a site of continued exploitation even after slavery's abolition in 1888. Local landowners claimed the territory, trapping residents in sharecropping arrangements where farmers received only a fraction of their harvest. Elder Marília dos Santos recalls how workers would lose two-thirds of their rice crop to landowners, with expenses further reducing their meager share. Today, delays in securing land titles expose the communities to new threats: shrimp farms encroaching on mangroves that sustain fishing and shellfish gathering, and increased river salinization affecting crops and drinking water.
This story matters because it illuminates how historical inequities persist in tangible ways, shaping lives and livelihoods across generations. Yet it's also a story of adaptation and determination—community members are pioneering pesticide-free farming, with one quilombo becoming Sergipe state's largest producer of agroecological rice. Their struggle intertwines cultural survival with environmental stewardship, offering a quiet testament to the power of collective resistance.

item.title: Camera at Iguaçu Falls captures jaguar cub 'acting cute' to get mother's attention, who joins in the play
item.description:
A camera trap at Iguaçu National Park, on the Argentine side of the famous waterfalls, captured a tender moment between a jaguar cub and its mother that reveals something deeper than simple play. The footage shows the young jaguar rolling on the ground, approaching its mother, and mock-attacking until she finally engages in the interaction—a scene that's both charming and scientifically significant.
The adult jaguar is Apepú, a female first identified in 2016, and this cub belongs to her second litter. The images were shared by the park and Project Yaguareté, which monitors the species in the region. While the behavior may look like innocent fun, researchers emphasize it serves a critical developmental purpose. During these playful exchanges, cubs learn essential survival skills they'll need as adults: how to move strategically, pursue prey, and defend themselves. Young jaguars typically stay with their mothers for eighteen to twenty-four months, a crucial apprenticeship period before venturing out on their own.
This footage represents more than a heartwarming wildlife moment. The presence of healthy cubs signals successful reproduction in the wild, an encouraging sign for a species that depends on preserved habitats, adequate prey populations, and connected corridors of Atlantic Forest to survive. In an era of habitat fragmentation and environmental pressures, watching a jaguar cub learn life's lessons from its mother offers quiet reassurance that conservation efforts can work—and that wild places still nurture the next generation.

item.title: Wing and a prayer: how probiotics might save bat species from a killer fungus
item.description:
A deadly fungus that has devastated bat populations across North America has now reached the northernmost known bat hibernation site in Canada's Northwest Territories, arriving sooner than scientists expected. White-nose syndrome, caused by the fungus Pseudogymnoascus destructans, attacks bats during hibernation, covering their faces and wings with a white growth that causes them to wake prematurely and burn through critical fat reserves. Since arriving in New York in 2007—likely on a caver's shoes from Europe—the disease has killed more than 6.7 million bats, wiping out 90% of little brown bats and 99% of northern long-eared bats in affected caves.
The Fort Smith caves, discovered in 2010 when a wildlife technician spotted distinctive karst landscape features from the air, shelter an estimated 3,000 bats and represent the largest hibernaculum in western Canada. These caves have been crucial for understanding how bats survive at extreme northern latitudes, where summers are short and cool. Researchers found that northern bats have adapted by taking more risks—flying at dusk rather than in full darkness and feeding on energy-rich orb-weaver spiders to build up reserves for the long winter.
This story matters because it captures scientists racing against time to understand and potentially save species pushed to the edge by an invasive pathogen. The researchers had hoped to study healthy populations before the fungus arrived, giving them a baseline for comparison and intervention. Now they're exploring whether probiotics might offer hope—a quiet but determined effort to find solutions for creatures that play vital roles in their ecosystems, reminding us how quickly the natural world can change and how much work remains to protect it.

item.title: Siraya gain recognition as Taiwan’s 17th official Indigenous group
item.description:
In a milestone decades in the making, the Siraya people of Taiwan have become the first Indigenous group from the island's lowland plains to gain official government recognition. On July 30, Premier Cho Jung-tai announced the Siraya as Taiwan's 17th legally recognized Indigenous group under the new Pingpu Indigenous Peoples Status Act, a law designed to acknowledge and redress centuries of cultural erasure. The moment was met with jubilation from community members, including activist Wan Cheng-hsiung, who exclaimed in Siraya, "We've finally come home."
The Siraya's journey to recognition reflects a larger historical pattern of forced assimilation. As a traditionally matrilineal society residing mainly around Tainan in southern Taiwan, they are the largest of the Pingpu groups—Indigenous communities from Taiwan's lowland plains and coastal areas. Unlike their highland counterparts, the Pingpu faced intense pressure to assimilate into Han Chinese culture under successive colonial powers, including the Qing dynasty, Japanese rule, and the Kuomintang government. Because they were perceived as "well assimilated," these communities were largely denied official status and the legal protections, resources, and cultural support that come with it. As of 2016, more than 11,800 people in Tainan were registered as Siraya.
Scholar Jolan Hsieh, who uses her Siraya name Bavaragh Dagalomai, emphasized that while recognition is profound, it's only a beginning. The designation carries concrete consequences—affecting political representation, language revitalization, land rights, and access to institutional support. This story matters because it captures a community's patient, multi-generational fight to restore what was taken from them: not just a legal status, but the dignity of being seen.

item.title: These Wetlands Treat the Wastewater of a Megacity
item.description:
Just outside Kolkata, India, a sprawling wetland performs an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. The East Kolkata Wetlands treat roughly 900 million liters of the city's wastewater daily—not through expensive technology, but through a centuries-old ecosystem of ponds, marshes, and farmland. Fish farmer Gagan Das wades into clear water that, hours earlier, was Kolkata's sewage, now transformed by sunlight, aquatic plants, and microbes into a thriving habitat where carp fatten on naturally filtered nutrients.
This 12,500-hectare site, recognized internationally as a Ramsar wetland, operates as what one ecologist calls "the largest natural waste recycling system in the world." Gravity carries wastewater from the city through underground pipes into a network of canals, where nature takes over. Solid waste settles into nutrient-rich sludge that becomes fertilizer for fields of sunflowers, eggplant, and tomatoes. Pollution-eating plants like water hyacinth and water spinach filter the water, while plankton and microbes break down organic matter, creating food for the fish that support over 30,000 families. The wetlands also absorb floodwater during monsoons, providing crucial protection for the densely populated region.
This story offers a quietly radical vision: that working with natural systems, rather than against them, can solve modern urban challenges. In an era when cities worldwide struggle with wastewater treatment costs and environmental degradation, the East Kolkata Wetlands demonstrate how traditional ecological knowledge—maintained by communities like those in Jamaipara village—can outperform high-tech infrastructure. It's a reminder that some of our most pressing problems already have solutions, written in the patient language of wetlands, microbes, and time.

item.title: Bringing the thrill of live music to deaf audiences – with the help of air guitar
item.description:
Luke Holdsworth, born profoundly deaf to deaf parents, spent his teenage years believing live concerts weren't meant for him. His first show didn't happen until his mid-twenties — a One Direction concert with no sign language interpretation, leaving him unable to follow along. Everything changed when he witnessed interpreter Tracey Tyer signing at a festival alongside the electronic group Underworld. The experience was revelatory, showing him that music could be fully accessible and deeply felt by deaf audiences when interpretation goes beyond literal translation to capture rhythm, emotion, and the artist's personality.
Now one of the UK's most respected British Sign Language interpreters at live events, Holdsworth has worked major performances including 14 dates on Oasis' reunion tour, shows for Lewis Capaldi and Harry Styles, and London's Pride celebrations. His approach treats interpretation as storytelling: he spends hours studying artists' back catalogs and the narratives behind songs, then uses his hearing aids' limited audio access combined with physical expression to convey tempo, melody, and stage presence. For Oasis, that meant embodying the Gallagher brothers' famous Mancunian swagger alongside colleague Samantha Vanterpool, bringing tens of thousands of deaf fans into the electric atmosphere at Cardiff's Principality Stadium.
This story quietly illuminates how access transforms experience. Holdsworth recalls seeing Madonna with full BSL interpretation and feeling, for once, like he didn't need to explain or advocate — just a young person enjoying a night out like anyone else. His work gives others what he missed growing up, turning concerts from inaccessible spectacles into shared cultural moments. It's a reminder that inclusion isn't just about meeting legal requirements; it's about ensuring everyone can feel the thrill of live music.

item.title: Demand for ethnic women’s refuge support nearly doubles in two years
item.description:
Shakti Women's Refuge, a New Zealand organization serving women from Asian, African, and Middle Eastern communities, has seen demand for its safe houses nearly double in the past two years. The Auckland-based group, founded in 1995 and now operating nationwide, provided more than 7,000 overnight spaces recently—up from roughly 3,600 in the previous two-year period. In response, Shakti opened a third safe house in Auckland last month, with facilities now consistently full.
The organization supports women facing family violence who often encounter additional barriers due to immigration status, cultural pressures, and community stigma. Strategic development manager Shasha Ali notes that while Shakti historically addressed culturally specific issues like dowry-related and honor-based violence, the profile of women seeking help has evolved to include highly educated individuals across varied backgrounds. A particularly stubborn obstacle remains the pressure around family honor and reputation, which can make seeking help feel like betraying one's community—concerns that persist whether someone is newly arrived or grew up in New Zealand. Despite three decades of service, Shakti is sometimes still labeled a "homewrecker," a characterization Ali firmly rejects, arguing there is no true home where abuse is tolerated.
This story matters because it illuminates how violence doesn't discriminate by education or status, and how cultural context shapes both the experience of abuse and the courage required to escape it. The doubling of demand reveals both a growing crisis and, perhaps more hopefully, an increasing willingness among women to reach out—a quiet but significant shift in communities where asking for help has long carried enormous social cost.

item.title: Ancestral lines united in Eastern Kuku Yalanji native title determination
item.description:
After a journey spanning three decades, the Eastern Kuku Yalanji people have achieved a landmark moment in their relationship with ancestral lands. The Federal Court has formally recognized their native title rights over 217,884 hectares of southeastern Cape York Peninsula in Queensland, an area that includes iconic landscapes like Cape Tribulation in the Daintree and Black Mountain near Cooktown. More than 600 traditional owners gathered in the Aboriginal community of Wujal Wujal to witness the historic determination.
What makes this achievement particularly remarkable is the unity it represents. The Eastern Kuku Yalanji brought together families from more than 100 ancestral lines to form the largest native title group on Cape York. The determination grants exclusive native title over about 35 percent of the area, meaning future activities will require permission from the traditional owners. The Jabalbina Yalanji Aboriginal Corporation will manage these rights, opening pathways for funding, land management, and opportunities for younger generations to connect with country.
This story resonates because it acknowledges both persistence and loss. The first claim was lodged in 1994, shortly after the Mabo decision created the legal framework for native title recognition. Many elders who began the fight did not live to see this day, a fact acknowledged by Chief Justice Debra Mortimer in her closing remarks. Yet the determination represents more than legal recognition—it offers the Eastern Kuku Yalanji people something profound: the freedom to simply be on their country without legal uncertainty, to practice culture, and to ensure their stories endure for generations to come.

item.title: After 17 years together, couple formalizes union in hospital during cancer treatment in Manaus
item.description:
After seventeen years together, José Maria Rodrigues de Pinho and Luciana de Souza Ferreira chose to formalize their union in a ceremony held at a hospital in Manaus, Brazil. José Maria, a 54-year-old truck driver, is currently receiving palliative care for pancreatic cancer that has metastasized to his liver. The couple, who met in 2009 and have a 10-year-old daughter, decided that now was the time to make their partnership official.
José began experiencing symptoms in December, but the cancer diagnosis wasn't confirmed until April. After complications during his third chemotherapy session in July, he has been hospitalized, including two stays in intensive care. Throughout these difficult months, Luciana has remained by his side. "I have never left him in any situation," she explained, describing their decision to formalize their union as both practical and emotional—a reaffirmation of the bond they've built over nearly two decades.
Hospital staff transformed a space within the facility for the civil ceremony, complete with cake, sweets, and decorations, allowing José to participate surrounded by the medical team caring for him. Despite his illness, José expressed gratitude for the moment and his determination to continue supporting his family. The story offers a quiet testament to enduring partnership—two people choosing to honor their commitment not in spite of hardship, but perhaps because of it, finding meaning in making official what their years together had already proven true.

item.title: Europe's first solar eclipse in 27 years in pictures
item.description:
Europe experienced its first total solar eclipse in nearly three decades, drawing millions of spectators from Spain to Iceland to witness the moon completely block the sun's light. The rare celestial event sparked widespread enthusiasm, with long queues forming outside shops selling specialized eclipse glasses—essential safety equipment that filters harmful solar radiation even when only a sliver of sun remains visible.
The eclipse's path crossed northern Spain and the Balearic Islands, where authorities anticipated up to 6 million visitors converging on mostly rural areas. In Reykjavik, watch parties erupted in cheers as darkness fell, while thousands gathered in town squares and on beaches across the continent. Spain's secretary of State for science expressed hope that the event would inspire a new generation of astrophysicists, calling it "such a special moment." The spectacle proved especially captivating in Spain, where the eclipse was followed immediately by sunset, creating a doubly dramatic display. Those outside the path of totality still enjoyed partial views, with landmarks from Paris to Saint Petersburg silhouetted against brilliant red and yellow skies.
This story offers a gentle reminder of our shared capacity for wonder. In an age of digital distraction, millions paused together to watch an ancient cosmic dance—the same phenomenon that has captivated humanity for millennia. It's a quietly hopeful portrait of collective curiosity, and a reminder that some experiences still draw us outside, looking upward, together.

item.title: Earthquake in Colombia: the film industry mobilizes at night to illuminate the rubble
item.description:
When a devastating 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, reducing buildings in the city of Cali to rubble and leaving neighborhoods in darkness, an unexpected group of professionals stepped forward to help. Film and audiovisual workers arrived at collapsed sites with the very tools of their trade—studio lights, generators, and production equipment—transforming disaster zones into illuminated workspaces where rescue operations could continue through the night.
The mobilization began spontaneously on Monday evening, organized through WhatsApp groups as the sun set around 6 p.m. and power outages plunged affected areas into darkness. Lighting technicians and cinematographers brought professional-grade equipment, while equipment rental companies donated gear free of charge. Sound engineers deployed sensitive directional microphones to listen for signs of life beneath the debris, and drone operators flew cameras overhead to search for survivors trapped in stairwells. Volunteers worked in continuous shifts, ensuring the lights never went dark during the critical 72-hour window when finding survivors is most likely. Some prepared food while others managed the rotation of generators and fuel supplies.
This story offers a quiet reminder of how specialized skills can serve urgent human needs in unexpected ways. The earthquake claimed at least 216 lives and injured over 2,000 people, but in the rubble of Cali, the same lights that once illuminated film sets now illuminated hope—a testament to community resourcefulness and the instinct to contribute whatever one has in moments of crisis.

item.title: 12th Brotas Gourmet Festival Brings Together Country Flavors, Music, and Attractions Over Four Days
item.description:
The Brazilian town of Brotas, in São Paulo state, is hosting its 12th annual Brotas Gourmet festival, a four-day celebration that weaves together regional cuisine, live music, and cultural pride. Running from Thursday through Sunday, this year's theme — "Tradition that Reinvents Itself: Flavors that Tell Stories" — invites thirteen local restaurants to craft original dishes inspired by comfort food traditions and made with ingredients sourced from the surrounding region. The festival aims to honor the town's culinary identity while providing an economic boost during the tourism off-season, supporting hotels, shops, and local businesses.
Beyond the food, the event showcases live performances from nine regional bands spanning genres from traditional sertanejo to Beatles covers, plus appearances by local breweries and distilleries. This year's edition also emphasizes sustainability, adopting a zero-waste approach with fully compostable packaging and environmental awareness campaigns woven throughout the weekend. The festival is organized by the local tourism association with support from the municipal government, reflecting a community-wide effort to celebrate what makes Brotas distinctive.
This story offers a snapshot of how smaller communities use food and culture to tell their own stories, build local economies, and reinvent tradition without abandoning it. It's a reminder that festivals can be more than entertainment — they can be acts of cultural preservation, economic strategy, and quiet innovation all at once.

item.title: Astronomers discover a new kind of cosmic object – a ‘black hole star’
item.description:
Astronomers have identified what they believe is an entirely new type of cosmic object: a "black hole star" that defies conventional categories. The discovery emerged when researchers investigating images from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope noticed an unusually brilliant red spot in the constellation Cetus, roughly 30 billion light years away. This object, which formed approximately 660 million years after the Big Bang, is as large as our entire solar system and radiates with extraordinary intensity.
What makes this finding remarkable is that the object produces 100 billion times more energy than any known star—an output characteristic of black holes—yet it displays properties typically associated with stars. Computer simulations suggest it's actually a black hole so thoroughly enveloped in dense gas that it glows like a star. The discovery may solve a long-standing puzzle: mysterious "Little Red Dots" that appear throughout deep space images might all be black hole stars rather than conventional celestial bodies.
This finding could reshape our understanding of cosmic evolution. Dr. Rohan Naidu and his team at MIT's Kavli Institute propose that black hole stars might be the early developmental stage of supermassive black holes, like the one anchoring our own Milky Way. If true, these objects play a fundamental role in galactic formation, influencing when stars form, when planets emerge, and ultimately when conditions become suitable for life. It's a reminder that even with our most advanced telescopes, the universe still holds categories of objects we're only beginning to recognize—each one potentially unlocking new chapters in the story of how everything came to be.

item.title: Psychologist transforms lives of socially vulnerable people through music: 'Welcomed and included'
item.description:
In Votuporanga, a city in São Paulo's interior, a 62-year-old psychologist and musician has found a remarkable way to bridge her two passions. Diná Freschi Ferreira created "Sons que Contam Histórias" (Sounds that Tell Stories), a project that uses music as a tool for connection and healing among people experiencing homelessness and social vulnerability. With more than 30 years teaching music and 12 years of psychology practice behind her, Ferreira recognized that music does far more than teach technical skills—it activates both hemispheres of the brain, processing melody while coordinating rhythm and movement, creating what she describes as a complete mental and physical exercise.
In 2025, partnering with Votuporanga's Cultural Department, Ferreira began walking through the city with her guitar, approaching people living on the streets. Where most saw only hardship, her psychology training helped her see individual stories waiting to be heard. Through rhythmic dynamics, group singing, percussion, and active listening, she created spaces where marginalized individuals could feel valued. The project has since expanded to include children, adults, and most recently, elderly residents of a local shelter, who formed their first choir together.
This story resonates because it demonstrates how combining professional skills with genuine compassion can restore dignity to those society often overlooks. Ferreira's greatest reward, she says, is witnessing the joy of people who finally feel welcomed and included—particularly elderly participants who still dream and remain deeply sensitive to each song. The project will be featured at Votuporanga's Literary Festival, bringing these often-forgotten voices to a wider audience and proving that sometimes the most powerful therapy comes not from a clinic, but from a shared melody.

item.title: On fragile Sumatran peatland, a farmer fights to bring back lost mangroves
item.description:
In a small village on Sumatra's northern coast, a palm oil farmer named Harisyah has spent fifteen years working to restore the mangrove forests that once protected his community. Now 53, he rises early to clear weeds and plant seedlings along the Siak River, driven by a personal conviction that local knowledge and persistence matter more than ambitious national targets. His village of Tanjung Kuras has watched its shoreline retreat by more than six meters annually, while increasingly erratic weather and tidal flooding remind residents of what they've lost. Last Ramadan, strong winds tore the dome off the village mosque—a stark symbol of the vanished forest buffer that once shielded the coast.
Harisyah's education in mangroves began in 2011 during an aquaculture course, where he discovered how these trees naturally filter water for fish ponds. What started as practical learning grew into a quiet mission. He visited restoration groups across the district, absorbing techniques and building relationships. Indonesia's coastline contains the world's largest mangrove estate, but decades of charcoal production and conversion to shrimp farms have degraded nearly half of it. The country's 2020 pledge to restore 600,000 hectares by 2024 captured global attention as perhaps the most ambitious reforestation effort ever attempted, yet only a fraction of the planned area was successfully planted.
This story matters because it illustrates a fundamental truth about environmental restoration: national ambitions falter without local champions. Harisyah represents a shift from top-down targets to grassroots perseverance, showing that meaningful change often begins with one person willing to stand knee-deep in peat, planting hope one stake at a time.

item.title: Nickel expansion puts Indonesia’s biodiversity goals under pressure, study finds
item.description:
Indonesia finds itself at a crossroads between two global imperatives: supplying nickel for the green energy transition and protecting some of Earth's most biodiverse ecosystems. A new study published in Nature Ecology & Evolution reveals that the country's nickel production has grown roughly tenfold over the past decade, positioning Indonesia to potentially supply nearly three-quarters of the world's nickel by 2040. This metal is essential not only for electric vehicle batteries but also for stainless steel, renewable energy infrastructure, and everyday items from kitchen cookware to construction materials.
The environmental stakes are significant. Researchers found that nearly half of projected global nickel demand through 2050 could be met by mines located in areas ranked among the world's top 10% for biodiversity and carbon conservation. For Indonesia, this creates a direct tension with its ambitious conservation commitments, including a pledge to protect 30% of its territory by 2030 and a goal to make its forestry and land-use sector carbon-neutral by the same year. Much of Indonesia's nickel comes from laterite deposits formed in tropical regions, where mining requires extensive land clearing that can fragment critical wildlife habitat across Sulawesi and the Maluku islands.
This story matters because it illustrates a paradox at the heart of the clean energy transition: the materials needed to build a sustainable future may come at a steep cost to the natural systems we're trying to protect. Indonesia's challenge is emblematic of a global dilemma, reminding us that environmental solutions often require difficult choices rather than easy answers.

item.title: Solar eclipse and the island of Ireland: The weather forecast and all you need to know
item.description:
Skywatchers across Ireland are preparing for a rare celestial treat: a deep partial solar eclipse on Wednesday that will obscure more than 90% of the sun—the most dramatic eclipse visible from the island until 2090. The timing is remarkable, as the eclipse will be followed just hours later by the peak of the Perseid meteor shower, creating what one astronomer describes as "celestial fireworks." For those traveling to Spain, a total eclipse lasting nearly two minutes awaits.
The eclipse will begin around 6:10 PM BST, with coverage varying by location. Belfast will see 93% of the sun covered, while Skellig Michael off the Kerry coast will experience nearly complete obscuration at 98%. Astronomers emphasize that even with such extensive coverage, the remaining sunlight remains dangerously bright—looking directly at it can damage the retina without any pain warning. Viewers are urged to use certified eclipse glasses or creative alternatives like pinhole viewers or even kitchen colanders to safely project the sun's image. The weather forecast offers mixed prospects, with cloud cover likely in parts of Northern Ireland while southern and eastern counties may enjoy clearer skies.
What makes this event quietly extraordinary is its rarity and the convergence of cosmic events in a single evening. For researchers like Ryan Milligan, who has traveled to Spain for his thirteenth eclipse, the experience transcends data and screens—it's described as visceral and emotional, a moment when day turns to night and the familiar world briefly transforms. For those staying home, even a partial eclipse offers a reminder of our place in a dynamic solar system, a spectacle that won't return in this form for seven decades.

item.title: Rare piglet the size of 'a grapefruit with legs' born at zoo
item.description:
A tiny babirusa piglet named Rana has made her public debut at Chester Zoo, offering a glimmer of hope for a species teetering on the brink of extinction. When she was born, keepers described her as roughly the size of a grapefruit with legs—a fitting image for one of nature's more unusual creatures. Babirusas, known as "pig-deer" in Malay due to their distinctive appearance, are found on only four Indonesian islands and face catastrophic decline in the wild, primarily due to African swine fever that reached their habitat five years ago.
Unlike most pigs, babirusas typically give birth to just one or two offspring at a time rather than large litters, making population recovery painfully slow. New mothers are also highly sensitive to disturbance, so keepers monitored Rana and her mother Matano remotely until they were ready for visitors. Matano herself was born at Chester Zoo eleven years ago and now has descendants across Europe, representing an important genetic safety net. The species, long classified as vulnerable, is being upgraded to critically endangered—a sobering reflection of how quickly their situation has deteriorated.
Beyond their quirky looks—males sport upper tusks that curve dramatically back toward their faces—babirusas play a crucial ecological role. As they forage, they disperse seeds that aid forest regeneration, making them vital to the health of island ecosystems. Conservationists describe Rana as a lifeline for her species and emphasize that her birth represents a race against time to prevent the loss of one of the oldest pig species still living. It's a quiet reminder that even the most charismatic and culturally significant creatures can vanish if we're not paying attention.

item.title: ‘It’s going to be spectacular’: Millions flock to Spain seeking best view of total solar eclipse
item.description:
Spain is preparing to host what may be one of the most-watched celestial events of the year: the country's first total solar eclipse in more than a century. A narrow band stretching roughly 200 kilometers from the northwest coast to Mallorca will experience totality on Wednesday, with officials estimating that up to 6 million people could gather along the path. While tens of millions across western Europe will witness a partial eclipse, Spain offers some of the best viewing conditions on mainland Europe, making it a magnet for eclipse chasers from around the world.
An estimated 460,000 visitors have traveled to Spain for the event, booking hotels months in advance and arriving from as far as Japan, the United States, and Canada. Among them is Angela Jones Rieksts from Halifax, who was moved to tears by her first total eclipse two years ago and now considers herself a devoted eclipse chaser. Preparations have been extensive: opticians and pharmacies sold out of eclipse glasses, Spanish airline Iberia organized a charter flight to view the phenomenon from 10,000 meters, and more than 24,000 police officers are being deployed to manage an expected 1.5 million additional car journeys. With temperatures forecast to reach 40°C and wildfire risks elevated, authorities are taking no chances.
This story captures a rare moment when millions pause to witness something larger than themselves—a celestial alignment that lasts less than two minutes but leaves lasting impressions. It's a reminder of how nature's grandest spectacles can still inspire awe, draw people across continents, and create shared experiences that transcend borders and everyday concerns.

item.title: Hiroshi Okuda, Toyota chair who pushed for the Prius, dies at 93
item.description:
Hiroshi Okuda, the visionary leader who guided Toyota Motor Corporation through a transformative period in the late 1990s and early 2000s, has passed away at 93. His tenure marked a significant shift for the Japanese automaker, as he became the first president from outside the founding family in a generation when he assumed the role in 1995.
Okuda's leadership style set him apart in Japan's often consensus-driven corporate culture. Tall, outspoken, and willing to take calculated risks, he pushed Toyota to embrace innovation at a time when the automotive industry stood on the cusp of major change. Under his guidance, the company launched the Prius, the pioneering gas-electric hybrid that would reshape global attitudes toward fuel efficiency and environmental responsibility in transportation. He also championed the RAV4 SUV, which became another commercial success. Beyond product development, Okuda earned recognition internally for his cost-cutting initiatives and decisive leadership, which he saw as essential antidotes to the bureaucratic inertia that can slow large corporations.
Okuda's career spanned the arc of Toyota's rise from a post-World War II manufacturer to a global automotive giant. His willingness to bet on unconventional technology like hybrid powertrains—when such vehicles were unproven in the marketplace—demonstrates a forward-thinking approach that helped position Toyota as an industry leader in sustainable transportation. This story reminds us how individual leadership and the courage to pursue untested ideas can shape entire industries and influence how millions of people move through the world.

item.title: UK to get best eclipse since 1999 as Moon blocks out Sun across Europe
item.description:
On Wednesday evening, the UK experienced its most significant solar eclipse since 1999—and the best the country will see for another half-century. Up to 96% of the Sun was covered by the Moon, with the peak occurring between 18:58 and 19:15 BST. Devon, Cornwall, and parts of Wales enjoyed the fullest views, while much of the country saw coverage exceeding 90%. Demand for eclipse glasses surged, with one London bakery selling around 100 pairs in a single morning.
Meanwhile, northern Spain, along with parts of Russia, Greenland, Iceland, and Portugal, witnessed a total eclipse. An estimated half a million visitors traveled to Spain for the event, gathering in cities like Bilbao, Valencia, and Palma to experience the minute and forty seconds of totality—when the Moon completely obscures the Sun and daylight briefly fades. Observers described the phenomenon as a chance to witness "the grandeur of nature," with families investing in the experience rather than "trivial things." Weather conditions were largely favorable across Spain, though some parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland faced cloudy skies.
Solar eclipses occur roughly every 18 months somewhere on Earth, but being in the path of totality—where the Moon's shadow falls—is rare for any given location. The UK won't see this level of coverage again until 2081, and a total eclipse won't grace British skies until 2090. For those fortunate enough to witness it, the event served as a humbling reminder of the celestial mechanics quietly unfolding above us, connecting strangers across continents in shared wonder.

item.title: 12yo will walk 500km for meeting with with prime minister in Canberra
item.description:
A twelve-year-old boy from Warren, a small town in western New South Wales, has decided to walk 500 kilometers to Australia's capital to advocate for better healthcare access for children in rural communities. Dusty Langby's ambitious 16-day trek to Parliament House isn't just symbolic—he's already raised $100,000 toward a $1 million goal for Little Wings, a charity that provides free flights to Sydney for rural children needing specialist care and brings pediatricians to remote communities.
The idea came to Dusty while swimming in his family's dam in January, a moment of inspiration that has since blossomed into a campaign with genuine impact. He and his brother have both benefited from Little Wings' services, being flown from Warren to Sydney for medical appointments, and Dusty wants other children to have the same opportunities. The funds he's raised so far can already provide a year of pediatric visits to five rural communities—care that would reach nearly 400 children. A team including the charity's CEO and local nurses will walk alongside him, and Dusty has secured something the organization itself never could: a meeting with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whom he plans to ask to match his fundraising total.
This story offers a quiet reminder that meaningful advocacy can come from anywhere, even from a twelve-year-old who's already worn through four pairs of training shoes. Dusty's determination highlights both the healthcare gaps facing rural Australia and the power of one person—however young—to mobilize attention and resources toward solving them.

item.title: Meet the Indigenous women restoring Kenya’s Mau Forest — and reshaping gender roles
item.description:
In the highlands of southwestern Kenya, a network of Indigenous women is quietly rewriting two stories at once: the future of the Mau Forest and their own roles within their communities. The Paran Women Group, founded in 2005, now connects 64 registered groups of mostly Maasai and Ogiek women across several counties. Through tree nurseries, beekeeping, kitchen gardens, and landscape restoration, these women are healing one of Kenya's most vital forest ecosystems while carving out new forms of independence and influence in their daily lives.
For many participants, the work represents a profound shift. Women like Judy Mukut balance conservation efforts with traditional domestic responsibilities—milking cattle, preparing meals, and caring for children—yet find time to gather at community resource centers where they raise seedlings, share ecological knowledge, and build new skills. Nancy Letina, who joined after her husband's death left her responsible for four children, describes how the program transformed her from complete economic dependence to self-sufficiency. Recent research supports this dual approach: a 2025 study found that restoration programs intentionally designed to address gender inequality not only empower women in household decision-making but also improve conservation outcomes over the long term.
This story matters because it illustrates how environmental restoration and social change can grow from the same soil. The women of Paran aren't waiting for permission or outside solutions—they're demonstrating that caring for forests and reshaping centuries-old gender roles can happen simultaneously, one seedling and one decision at a time.

item.title: A little-remembered Gilded Age millionaire helped make milk safe for American kids through his ‘retail giving’
item.description:
In a time when philanthropists like Rockefeller and Carnegie set sweeping goals to benefit all humanity, one wealthy businessman took a different path. Nathan Straus, co-owner of Macy's department store, focused his charitable energy on a modest but urgent problem: making milk safe for children to drink. His story, explored in Andrew Fisher's new biography, offers a compelling case for what might be called "retail giving"—philanthropy with humble, practical aims that can nonetheless save thousands of lives.
Straus came from a German Jewish family that immigrated to America in the 1850s. After establishing themselves in Georgia, the Civil War disrupted their business and pushed them north to New York City. There, the Straus brothers built a thriving business selling china and glassware, eventually partnering with and then fully acquiring Macy's during the retailing revolution of the late 19th century. While his brother Isidor managed store operations and another brother Oscar entered politics, Nathan handled external affairs and increasingly turned his attention to public health causes, particularly championing the pasteurization of milk at a time when contaminated dairy was a deadly threat to children.
This story matters because it quietly challenges our assumptions about effective philanthropy. While grand visions capture the history books, Straus demonstrated that targeting a single, solvable problem—ensuring children had access to safe milk—could create profound change. His approach stands as a reminder that transformative giving doesn't always require worldwide ambitions; sometimes the most meaningful impact comes from addressing the immediate, overlooked needs right in front of us.

item.title: Lebanon parliament votes to end death penalty, 1st in Middle East to do so
item.description:
Lebanon has become the first country in the Middle East to formally abolish the death penalty, with parliament voting to replace capital punishment with life imprisonment and aggravated hard labor. The decision transforms what had been an unofficial moratorium on executions—in place since 2004—into permanent legal protection. At the time of the vote, 85 people were facing death sentences in Lebanon.
The legislation passed with majority support in the 128-member assembly, though Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc opposed the measure. Justice Minister Adel Nassar called it a "historic step," and human rights organizations praised the move as a significant milestone for the region. Amnesty International noted that Lebanon is now aligned with a global trend toward abolition, turning a temporary pause in executions into lasting human rights progress. However, practical questions remain about how the new punishment of aggravated hard labor will actually be enforced, given Lebanon's resource constraints and overcrowded prisons.
The timing is complex: parliament is simultaneously debating a broad amnesty law that could reduce sentences or release individuals convicted of violent offenses—the largest such amnesty since Lebanon's civil war ended in 1990. This has drawn protests from families of victims, some of whom had hoped to see perpetrators executed rather than granted reduced sentences. The story offers a window into how societies navigate competing values around justice, mercy, and human rights, even amid practical challenges and deep disagreements about what accountability should look like.

item.title: Lunar calendar: Mayan book predicted eclipses a thousand years ago
item.description:
A thousand years ago, Maya astronomers created something that continues to astonish modern scientists: a lunar calendar so precise it could predict solar eclipses across centuries. The Dresden Codex, one of the oldest surviving books in the Americas, contains an intricate system that tracked the moon's cycles and anticipated eclipses with remarkable accuracy—all without telescopes, computers, or modern physics.
What makes this achievement particularly impressive is how the Maya solved a problem that plagues all lunar calendars: the moon's cycles don't align perfectly with solar years, causing errors to accumulate over time. The Maya developed what researchers now recognize as a kind of ancestral "algorithmic thinking," creating a system that combined different lunar cycles and included periodic corrections to keep the calendar synchronized. Through patient observation spanning generations and ingenious calculations, they built a tool that could forecast virtually every solar eclipse visible from Maya territories between 350 and 1150 CE, with an error margin of only about one hour.
This story offers a quiet reminder of the sophistication of ancient scientific thinking. The Dresden Codex reveals a culture deeply invested in understanding celestial patterns, not through sudden flashes of genius, but through methodical observation, careful record-keeping, and mathematical innovation passed down across generations. It's a testament to what human curiosity and persistence can achieve, even without the technology we now take for granted.

item.title: ‘I feel motherly towards them’: the nature reserve manager sharing her office with a wasp nest
item.description:
When a wasp colony moved into Eilish Rothney's office at a Norfolk nature reserve, her initial impulse to remove them gave way to curiosity. The reserve manager decided to share her workspace with the expanding nest, which now towers over a metre tall and blankets an entire bookshelf in intricate layers of chewed wood pulp. What began as an unwelcome intrusion became an unexpected cohabitation experiment.
Rothney adapted her routine to accommodate her new officemates, opening a window to give them a clear flight path and moving calmly through the space. She describes the nest as almost a living organism itself, emitting a low purring sound from thousands of wings beating to regulate temperature. Her observations reveal the colony's remarkable dynamics: a queen laying eggs continuously, workers foraging and feeding larvae, and a complex exchange of nutrients that keeps the system running. Rather than fear stings, Rothney believes insects recognize individuals who mean them no harm, advocating for calm coexistence.
Her tolerance extends beyond her own office to defending the wasps that crash summer picnics. She explains that late-summer aggression stems from desperation—adult workers suddenly cut off from their main food source when larvae stop producing sugary secretions. As autumn approaches and the colony's natural lifecycle winds down, Rothney admits she'll feel motherly sadness when her temporary colleagues depart. This quiet story matters because it challenges our reflexive hostility toward creatures we've labeled pests, suggesting that understanding and patience might replace convenience-driven extermination. It's a gentle reminder that coexistence, even with wasps, is often more rewarding than we imagine.

item.title: First in her family to speak English, Brazilian overcomes competition from 33,000 candidates and wins World Bank internship
item.description:
Gabrielle Hayashi Santos, a young woman from Bauru in the interior of São Paulo, Brazil, has achieved something quietly extraordinary: securing one of 120 internship positions at the World Bank, competing against nearly 33,000 candidates. What makes her story particularly striking is that she's the first in her family to speak English, earn a postgraduate degree, or study abroad—milestones born from determination rather than privilege.
Growing up, international exchanges seemed impossibly distant. Her father left school in elementary grades to work various jobs—collecting cans, driving trucks, working as a mechanic—only completing high school when Gabrielle was six. Her mother, a pharmacist of Japanese descent, moved from a small agricultural town in Mato Grosso to attend university. The family's only connection to the world beyond Brazil was relatives traveling to Japan for factory work to send money home. Yet Gabrielle discovered through persistent research that scholarships could open doors she'd assumed were closed. Starting in high school, she won funding for courses abroad in leadership and entrepreneurship. Her mother initially worried the opportunities might be scams, but gradually came to trust the programs. Gabrielle went on to study International Relations, complete a master's in Germany, and intern at UNESCO, focusing on how careers can transform not just individuals but entire families.
Her story offers something worth pausing over: a reminder that ambitious paths aren't reserved for those born into them. Gabrielle's achievement isn't just about personal success—it's about expanding what seems possible, one generation opening doors the previous couldn't have imagined, and the quiet persistence required to cross thresholds that once seemed firmly shut.

item.title: Three sports groups using movement to tackle isolation
item.description:
Three grassroots organizations are demonstrating how physical activity can become a bridge out of loneliness and isolation, offering something deeper than conventional fitness programs. Sport in Mind, founded in 2010 to help one unwell friend, has now supported more than 60,000 people experiencing mental health challenges through free sessions ranging from football and walking to gardening and dance. Rather than emphasizing competition, the charity works with the NHS and community partners to create welcoming environments where movement becomes a pathway to routine, confidence, and recovery.
The Bluetits Chill Swimmers takes a different approach, building a global volunteer-led community around cold water swimming and dipping. What started in Wales has expanded into informal local groups where the focus isn't endurance or performance, but the simple pleasure of being in nature together, gently challenging oneself, and finding companionship through shared ritual. Meanwhile, GoodGym combines exercise with practical community service, connecting runners, walkers, and cyclists with local projects and isolated older people who need help with tasks like garden clearing or home projects.
What makes these initiatives quietly remarkable is their recognition that movement doesn't have to be solitary or competitive to be valuable. By weaving physical activity together with connection, purpose, and service, they're transforming exercise from an individual pursuit into something that strengthens entire communities while addressing the very real challenges of loneliness and mental health that many people face today.

item.title: To No Longer Bow Our Heads: Searching for the Disappeared of the Spanish Civil War (3/4)
item.description:
Ninety years after the Spanish Civil War began, thousands of families are still searching for their missing loved ones. More than 100,000 people remain unidentified, the vast majority victims of Francoist repression. Recent excavations are finally allowing descendants to recover remains and provide dignified burials—bringing closure to wounds that have spanned generations.
The story of Antonio Carrascal Lema illustrates this long journey toward peace. An agricultural worker and municipal councilor affiliated with the socialist workers' union, he was executed by rebel forces in September 1936. For ninety years, his granddaughter Adela knew little about his fate. The trauma ran deep, silenced by pain and official obstruction—when the family sought information, they were told archives had been burned. In 2024, a phone call changed everything: excavations in Zufre's cemetery uncovered nine bodies, and DNA testing with Antonio's still-living daughter confirmed his identity. "He now rests in peace. We have triumphed over forgetting," Adela said at the May 2026 ceremony where she finally laid him to rest beside his wife.
The Spanish Civil War claimed at least 500,000 lives between 1936 and 1939, with repercussions lasting until 1948. While bodies of those executed by Republicans were exhumed and returned to families after the war, Francoist victims were left in unmarked graves and mass burial sites. This story matters because it reveals how historical wounds persist across generations when truth remains buried, and how the simple act of knowing—of finally being able to name and honor the dead—can bring dignity back to families who were forced to bow their heads for far too long.

item.title: Perseid meteor shower reaches peak: When and where to catch a glimpse
item.description:
The Perseids meteor shower, widely considered the best annual celestial display, reaches its peak this week, offering skywatchers a chance to see up to 100 shooting stars per hour. This year brings an unusual bonus: a deep partial solar eclipse visible in the UK will occur just hours before the meteor shower begins, creating what astronomer Dr. Becky Smethurst calls "the perfect cosmic coincidence of events." The Perseids are caused by debris from the Swift-Tuttle comet, a massive object with a 16-mile solid core that takes 133 years to orbit the Sun, meaning some of the burning fragments may have been left behind more than a century ago.
While the Perseids are active from mid-July through late August, the prime viewing window falls in the early morning hours of August 12-13, between midnight and dawn. This year offers especially favorable conditions due to the new moon, which means no competing moonlight to wash out fainter meteors. For the best experience, observers should seek locations away from city lights, allow their eyes 20-30 minutes to adjust to darkness, and look toward the widest possible expanse of sky. England and Wales are expected to have clear skies, while Scotland and Northern Ireland may contend with more cloud cover.
This story offers a gentle reminder to look up and reconnect with the cosmos. The Perseids provide a rare chance to witness ancient debris burning up in real time, connecting us to celestial events that unfold on timescales far beyond human lifespans—what Smethurst aptly describes as "the Universe's own cosmic clock."

item.title: Indigenous artist travels 600 km to exhibit Karipuna body art at Amapá Expo: 'Representing my people is priceless'
item.description:
A 28-year-old Karipuna artist traveled more than 600 kilometers from his indigenous territory in Brazil's far north to share his people's traditional body art at a cultural exposition in Macapá. Eddír Iaparrá Karipuna's journey from the Uaçá Indigenous Land in Oiapoque required long hours by road and river, but for him, the opportunity to represent his community carried meaning beyond measure.
At the Expofeira 2026, Eddír paints traditional geometric patterns on visitors' skin using natural ink made from genipap fruit and charcoal. Each design carries ancestral significance—the spiral, for example, serves as a protective amulet against negative energy. For indigenous peoples, these body graphics function as a visual language expressing identity, spirituality, and connection to nature, acting both as markers of belonging and symbolic shields. The experience draws curious visitors, including a tourist from Pernambuco who had always wanted body art but feared needles, and found the temporary natural ink painting a beautiful alternative.
The artist, who is also a musician and composer, emphasizes that his presence represents countless community members who couldn't make the difficult journey. The indigenous pavilion at the free nine-day exposition features representatives from seven Amapá ethnic groups, showcasing feather earrings, natural accessories, and handcrafted objects. This story quietly illuminates how cultural traditions traverse distance and time, finding new audiences while maintaining their sacred meanings—a reminder that preservation and sharing need not be contradictory, and that sometimes the greatest honor lies simply in showing up for one's people.

item.title: Jackie, a beloved bald eagle and livestream star, dies of mysterious illness
item.description:
Jackie, a bald eagle who became an unlikely internet sensation through a livestream of her nest at California's Big Bear Lake, has died at age 14 from an unidentified illness. The eagle had been receiving care at the Ojai Raptor Center since mid-July, when she was found weak and unable to fly following an altercation with younger eagles. Despite extensive testing including CT scans and bone marrow biopsies, veterinary experts were unable to determine the cause of her severe anemia.
Millions of viewers worldwide had followed Jackie's life since the livestream began in 2015, initially watching her parents before Jackie herself took over the nest in 2018. Her partnership with Shadow, her mate, became particularly popular during the pandemic as audiences watched them raise multiple clutches of chicks. This year brought both heartbreak and joy: ravens consumed their first two eggs in January, but Jackie laid replacements in February, successfully hatching Luna and Sandy. The latter was named in honor of a recently deceased conservationist.
Jackie's influence extended far beyond entertainment. Her presence sparked a remarkable $10 million conservation effort by Friends of Big Bear Lake to purchase 63 acres near her nest that had been threatened by development. The campaign drew support from local schoolchildren to tech entrepreneurs, demonstrating how a single wild creature can galvanize environmental action. Jackie's story reminds us that sometimes the most powerful conservation ambassadors are simply living their lives while we watch—and in watching, we learn to care deeply about protecting the wild spaces they call home.

item.title: Yarning circles raise concerns about repetition of Stolen Generations
item.description:
In South Australia, nearly 40 percent of children in out-of-home care are Aboriginal, despite Aboriginal people making up a small fraction of the population. Carers and community members are raising alarm that this disproportionate representation echoes the trauma of the Stolen Generations, particularly as many children are losing connection to their culture, language, and land. South Australia has the second-highest rate of children in out-of-home care nationally, and Aboriginal children there are placed in care at a rate significantly higher than the national average.
An Aboriginal-led organization called KWY has launched a four-year research project, Wilto Willo—meaning "spring star" in the Kaurna language—to gather community voices and develop solutions. Through yarning circles in Port Lincoln, Port Augusta, and Adelaide, about 200 carers have shared their experiences. They report systemic issues including high staff turnover, fly-in fly-out workers, long waits for medical and psychological assessments, and a failure to follow Aboriginal placement principles, which prioritize keeping children connected to family and culture. Some children have gone six months without a support worker, and many have been placed in non-Indigenous homes where they've had little opportunity to learn their heritage or visit country.
This story matters because it highlights an urgent question: despite policies aimed at closing the gap and protecting Aboriginal children's rights, why are the numbers worsening? The research suggests that most child protection funding goes toward intervening after harm, rather than preventing it. By centering Aboriginal voices and community-led solutions, Wilto Willo offers a path forward—one that honors identity, belonging, and the hard lessons of history.

item.title: Quitting dream job over climate fears a 'no-brainer' for former pilot
item.description:
After four decades as a commercial pilot and 25,000 hours in the sky, Geoff Collis made an unexpected career change driven by climate concerns. The former Jetstar pilot, who fell in love with aviation at age ten, found himself increasingly troubled by the environmental cost of his dream job—ordering 2.4 million liters of jet fuel annually. When COVID-19 grounded much of the industry, the then-55-year-old began an apprenticeship at a local Melbourne bakery, discovering unexpected fulfillment in the craft of bread and pastry making.
Though he briefly returned to flying in 2023 when the aviation sector recovered, Collis ultimately decided he could no longer reconcile his work with his climate conscience. He described much of the industry's environmental efforts as "tokenism, spin and greenwashing," making his departure feel inevitable. Aviation presents a unique environmental challenge: while responsible for only two to three percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, it's one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize. The International Civil Aviation Organization projects emissions could increase two to five times 2018 levels by 2070, even as other industries reduce their carbon footprints. Airlines like Qantas acknowledge operating on growth models while investing in sustainable aviation fuel and newer aircraft.
This story resonates because it captures a deeply personal response to a global dilemma—what happens when passion and principle collide? Collis's choice represents the kind of difficult reckoning many may face as climate realities deepen, and his transition from cockpit to kitchen suggests that meaningful work can be found in unexpected places, even when it means leaving behind the dream of a lifetime.

item.title: Measles returns to spark alert in Brazil: who needs to get vaccinated? See questions and answers about the disease
item.description:
Brazil is experiencing a renewed measles alert, with 24 confirmed cases reported as of early February—23 in São Paulo state and one in Rio de Janeiro. The resurgence comes amid a broader measles outbreak across the Americas, including the largest surge in the United States in 35 years. Health experts point to declining vaccination rates, fueled partly by misinformation and anti-vaccine movements, as the primary reason the virus has regained a foothold in communities with insufficient immunity.
Brazil only recently regained its measles elimination certification in 2024, and while the current case count is far lower than outbreaks in other countries, officials are taking the situation seriously. The cases have been traced to imported infections, many linked to international travel, including Brazilians returning from the World Cup in countries with higher case numbers. In response, cities like São Paulo, Guarulhos, and São Bernardo do Campo are offering measles vaccines to everyone aged six months to 59 years, regardless of vaccination history, to break potential transmission chains.
The story offers a window into how infectious diseases respect no borders and how quickly progress can be reversed without vigilant public health measures. Measles is not a mild illness—it spreads with remarkable ease, and the virus can cause serious complications affecting the lungs and nervous system. As international travel rebounds, this quiet alarm in Brazil underscores the importance of maintaining high vaccination coverage to protect communities and preserve hard-won public health achievements.

item.title: Dogs can distinguish between fearful and angry or sad human faces, brain scans suggest
item.description:
Dogs may be more attuned to human emotions than previously understood. New research using brain imaging has revealed that canine brains can distinguish not only between happy and unhappy human faces, but also between different types of negative expressions—a ability researchers say represents the first demonstration that dogs can differentiate emotions of the same emotional valence.
In the study, researchers at the University of Vienna trained pet dogs to lie still in MRI scanners while viewing photographs of unfamiliar human faces displaying various emotions. Initial experiments showed increased brain activity in areas associated with visual processing, social cognition, and reward when dogs viewed happy faces compared to neutral ones. A second experiment involving twelve dogs and four different expressions—happiness, sadness, fear, and anger—revealed something more nuanced: while certain brain regions could distinguish happy from any negative expression, distinguishing between different unhappy faces required analyzing activity across the entire brain. The dogs' brains could tell fearful faces apart from angry or sad ones, though anger and sadness proved harder to differentiate from each other. Researchers suggest this may reflect how different negative expressions signal different types of threats, and that dogs might need additional cues like body language to make finer distinctions.
This research offers a window into how thousands of years of domestication have shaped dogs' remarkable sensitivity to human communication. Beyond satisfying curiosity about our companions' inner lives, the findings suggest practical applications—such as using positive facial expressions to enhance training—and remind us that the bond between humans and dogs runs deeper than we might see on the surface.

item.title: In Côte d'Ivoire, biama has all the youth dancing
item.description:
In the bustling streets of Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire, a new dance and music phenomenon has captured the hearts of young people across the nation. Born just five years ago in Yopougon—the city's poorest yet most vibrant district—biama has become a cultural force that speaks to a generation. The style pulses with energy, moving even faster than coupé-décalé, an earlier Ivorian genre known for its association with glamorous nightclubs and flashy displays.
