What sets biama apart is its accessibility and democratic spirit. While coupé-décalé belonged to exclusive nightclub culture, biama thrives in open spaces—street corners, public squares, and smartphone screens. Young dancers, known as biamasseurs, share their moves on TikTok and other social platforms, building vast audiences without the backing of traditional record labels. The most popular performers have achieved remarkable success, amassing millions of views online and embarking on tours across Europe and Africa, all while staying rooted in the grassroots culture that birthed the movement.
This story offers a window into how creativity flourishes in unexpected places and how digital platforms have reshaped the landscape of cultural expression. Biama represents more than just dance steps and rhythms; it's a testament to young people claiming public space, building community, and creating opportunities outside conventional industry structures. In a world often focused on top-down cultural production, here's a movement rising from the streets, connecting a generation through joy, movement, and shared identity.

item.title: August will have two eclipses, but only one can be seen from Brazil
item.description:
August brings a rare celestial double feature: two eclipses within the same month, each visible from different parts of the world. While a total solar eclipse will grace the Northern Hemisphere on August 12th, it's the second event—a partial lunar eclipse on August 28th—that will capture the attention of skywatchers across Brazil and much of the Americas, Europe, and Africa.
The solar eclipse occurs when the Moon positions itself precisely between the Sun and Earth, casting its shadow across the planet. This month's total eclipse will trace a path across Greenland, Iceland, northern Russia, Spain, and a small portion of Portugal, with partial views available across much of Europe. Unfortunately for South American observers, the phenomenon won't be visible at all from Brazil. But the lunar eclipse later in the month offers everyone a chance to participate. Beginning at 1 a.m. local time on August 28th, the event will be visible to the naked eye throughout all Brazilian states, requiring no special equipment or travel to remote viewing locations.
This story reminds us that the universe operates on its own schedule, occasionally offering us two celestial performances in a single month. While one eclipse passes by unseen, the other arrives as an invitation—a chance to look up in the predawn darkness and witness Earth's shadow gently crossing the Moon's face, connecting observers across continents in a shared moment of wonder.

item.title: Boa constrictor rescued by firefighters from inside speaker in Ceará; video
item.description:
In the coastal town of Aracati, Brazil, a couple transporting sound equipment for their evangelical band made an unexpected discovery: a boa constrictor had taken up residence inside one of their speakers. The mystery began when the husband noticed something shifting inside the equipment during transport last Saturday. What should have been routine setup for a performance turned into a curious wildlife encounter.
When a sound technician opened the speaker cabinet at the couple's shop, he found the snake coiled inside the speaker housing. Rather than attempt removal themselves, the owners wisely contacted local firefighters, who safely extracted the serpent without harm to animal or humans. The most puzzling aspect of the situation remains unsolved: no one knows how the boa entered the equipment, when it arrived, or how long it had been living there. According to owner Valéria Vilck, the speaker had been in regular use, vibrating with music while its stowaway remained hidden and undetected.
This story offers a gentle reminder of how wildlife and human spaces intersect in unexpected ways, even in the most unlikely places. There's something quietly remarkable about a snake finding shelter in an instrument meant to amplify sound, surviving unnoticed amid the very vibrations that might have driven other creatures away. It's a small tale that speaks to both the adaptability of nature and the importance of responding to such surprises with care rather than panic.

item.title: Rare visitor: only semi-albino female southern right whale recorded since 1987 sighted in Santa Catarina; VIDEO
item.description:
Off the coast of Santa Catarina, Brazil, researchers have documented a remarkable return visitor: the only known semi-albino female southern right whale recorded in the country since cataloging began in 1987. The whale, designated B-964, was first identified in August 2023 swimming with her calf near the beaches of Garopaba and Imbituba. Her distinctive gray skin marked with black patches makes her unmistakable among her species.
Semi-albinism is exceptionally rare in southern right whales, occurring in only about 3% of individuals worldwide. Of the 38 semi-albino whales documented in Brazil's photo-identification catalog over nearly four decades, B-964 is the sole female. The coloration results from a recessive genetic variation—both parents must carry the gene for a semi-albino calf to be born. These whales are born white and gradually develop their characteristic gray coloring as they mature. When B-964 was spotted again in July 2024, she was swimming alone in waters known as a natural nursery for the species. Researchers suspect she may have returned to give birth, as southern right whales typically bear calves every three years.
This story offers a quiet window into the careful, patient work of marine conservation. The researchers' hope to spot B-964 with a new calf reflects decades of dedication to understanding individual whales through distinctive physical markers like head callosities and body patterns. It's a reminder that even among creatures as vast and ancient as whales, individuals matter—and that persistence in observation can reveal the exceptional hidden within the everyday rhythms of migration and reproduction.

item.title: Real estate agent offers to repair 20 public housing homes for free
item.description:
A Canberra real estate agent who once experienced homelessness himself is mobilizing an unusual solution to a troubling gap in public housing. Jonny Warren, who lived on the streets as a teenager while struggling with addiction, has launched a campaign to repair 20 vacant government-owned homes before Christmas—all pro bono. His motivation came from a visceral encounter during a charity patrol: seeing a mother and her four-year-old sleeping in a car.
The numbers behind Warren's initiative highlight a frustrating paradox. More than 580 public housing properties sit empty in the Australian Capital Territory, with 285 requiring repairs before they can welcome tenants. Meanwhile, over 3,650 approved applicants languish on the waiting list—some for more than five years. Warren has already assembled a volunteer army of tradespeople ready to tackle the work, which ranges from deep cleaning to installing new carpets and fixtures. He describes many of the properties as needing only "final little touches" rather than major overhauls.
While housing advocates welcome the effort, they caution that dignified, quality repairs require more than quick fixes. Independent legislator Thomas Emerson is backing the plan and pressing the government to support it, calling the vacancy situation "insane" amid such acute need. Warren's story illustrates how personal experience can spark creative community action, while also raising questions about why systemic gaps persist when willing hands are ready to help. It's a reminder that sometimes the resources to solve a problem are already present—they just need coordination and permission to act.

item.title: Italy’s record-low Po River forces farmers to weigh crop switch
item.description:
Italy's Po River, the lifeblood of the country's industrial heartland, is swinging between devastating extremes as climate change disrupts centuries of predictable water supply. The 652-kilometer waterway, which rises in the Alps and flows to the Adriatic, supports nearly 41% of Italy's GDP and a third of its agricultural output. Now, farmers like Massimo Salvagnin face an unsettling calculation: whether planting seeds will result in crops or simply cook them in superheated soil.
The river recently fell to a record low at Cremona, dropping below even the severe 2022 drought mark, with flow reduced to less than a third of normal levels. Yet the challenge isn't only drought. Spring snowmelt can send 10 billion cubic meters of water past Ferrara in under two weeks, while months later the same region scrambles for every drop. Infrastructure manager Stefano Calderoni operates 4,200 kilometers of canals and 160 pumps to manage farmland reclaimed from marshes, much of it below sea level. The system was designed for nature's predictable rhythms, not today's volatile swings between flood and drought.
This story offers a window into how climate change is quietly rewriting the rules for regions built on assumptions of stability. It's not about distant projections or abstract models, but about a farmer standing in his field, seeds in hand, forced to gamble on whether the ground itself has become too hostile for life to take root. The Po's transformation speaks to a broader question facing communities everywhere: how to adapt systems designed for one climate reality to survive in another.
